cse-2024-2-cs-43.approach: The 3000 sectors are scattered randomly, so **every sector is a separate access**: seek + average rotational latency + one-sector transfer. Compute that per-sector time once and multiply by 3000.
cse-2024-2-cs-43.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| rotation | 6000 RPM |
| average seek | 5 ms |
| sectors/track | 500 |
| sector size | 512 B (not needed) |
| file | 3000 randomly placed sectors |

steps.title: Rotation time and average rotational latency
steps.body:
$$6000\ \text{RPM}=\frac{6000}{60}=100\ \text{rotations/s}\ \Rightarrow\ T_{rot}=\frac{1}{100}\ \text{s}=10\ \text{ms}.$$
Average rotational latency is half a rotation: $\frac{10}{2}=5$ ms.

steps.title: Transfer time of one sector
steps.body:
One rotation passes all 500 sectors of a track under the head, so one sector takes
$$\frac{10\ \text{ms}}{500}=0.02\ \text{ms}.$$

steps.title: Time for one random sector
steps.body:
Because the sectors are located randomly, each read needs its own seek and its own rotational wait:
$$t_{\text{sector}}=\underbrace{5}_{\text{seek}}+\underbrace{5}_{\text{latency}}+\underbrace{0.02}_{\text{transfer}}=10.02\ \text{ms}.$$

cse-2024-2-cs-43.shortcut: Per random sector $\approx$ seek $+$ half a rotation $= 5+5=10$ ms (transfer $0.02$ ms is tiny) → $3000\times10.02$ ms $\approx 30.06$ s.
pitfalls: Treating the file as contiguous (one seek + one latency + $3000\times0.02=60$ ms) gives $\approx0.07$ s — wrong, the sectors are **random**.
Using a full rotation (10 ms) as latency instead of the average half rotation gives $3000\times15.02$ ms $=45.06$ s.
The 512-byte sector size is a distractor: transfer time per sector follows directly from 500 sectors per rotation.
cse-2024-2-cs-43.verification: Units check: $10.02\ \text{ms}\times3000=30\,060$ ms. Bounds: ignoring transfer gives exactly $30.00$ s, and transfer adds $3000\times0.02=60$ ms → $30.06$ s, inside the key range $29.50$–$30.50$.

cse-2024-2-cs-44.approach: A **timeout** (not triple duplicate ACKs) makes TCP halve the threshold and restart **slow start** from 1 MSS; then the window doubles every fully acknowledged RTT until it reaches the threshold.

steps.title: Reaction to the timeout
steps.body:
On a timeout TCP sets
$$\text{ssthresh}=\frac{\text{cwnd}}{2}=\frac{12}{2}=6\ \text{MSS},\qquad \text{cwnd}=1\ \text{MSS}.$$
So the **first RTT** after the timeout sends with $\text{cwnd}=1$.

steps.title: Second RTT: slow start doubles the window
steps.body:
All segments of RTT 1 are acknowledged and $1<6$, so slow start applies (+1 MSS per ACK, i.e. doubling per RTT):
$$\text{cwnd}=1\times2=2\ \text{MSS}.$$

steps.title: Third RTT
steps.body:
All segments of RTT 2 are acknowledged and $2<6$, still slow start:
$$\text{cwnd}=2\times2=4\ \text{MSS}\quad(4<6,\ \text{threshold not yet reached}).$$
The window during the third RTT is **4 MSS**.

cse-2024-2-cs-44.shortcut: After a timeout the RTT-$k$ window is $2^{k-1}$ MSS while below ssthresh: $2^{3-1}=4\ (<6)$.
pitfalls: Treating the loss like 3 duplicate ACKs (fast recovery, cwnd $=6$) — that is only for duplicate-ACK loss detection, not a timeout.
Counting one doubling too many and answering 8 — the first RTT after the timeout already uses cwnd $=1$.
Switching to linear growth too early: congestion avoidance starts only when cwnd reaches ssthresh $=6$.
cse-2024-2-cs-44.verification: Windows per RTT: $1, 2, 4$; all below ssthresh $=6$, so pure doubling is correct. The 4th RTT would be $\min(8,\ 6)$ → 6 and then linear growth — consistent with the rules.

cse-2024-2-cs-45.approach: For CSMA/CD the sender must still be transmitting when news of a collision at the far end returns, so $T_{\text{frame}}\ge 2\,T_{\text{prop}}$; multiply that time by the bit rate.
cse-2024-2-cs-45.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| bandwidth $B$ | $10^8$ bits/s |
| max length $d$ | 500 m |
| signal speed $v$ | $2\times10^8$ m/s |

steps.title: Worst case: collision at the far end
steps.body:
A station at one end starts; just before its first bit reaches the other end ($t\approx T_p$), the far station starts too. The collision signal needs another $T_p$ to come back. The first station must still be transmitting then:
$$T_{\text{frame}}\ge 2T_p=5\ \mu\text{s}.$$

steps.title: Convert time to bits
steps.body: $$L_{\min}=B\times2T_p=10^8\times5\times10^{-6}=500\ \text{bits}.$$

pitfalls: Using one-way delay only ($T_p$) gives 250 bits — the collision signal must also travel back.
Misreading the flattened exponents (e.g. $10^8$ as 108) gives nonsense values.
cse-2024-2-cs-45.verification: Transmitting 500 bits at $10^8$ bit/s takes $500/10^8=5\ \mu$s, exactly the round-trip time $2\times2.5\ \mu$s.

cse-2024-2-cs-46.approach: A useful FD is an **ordered pair of disjoint non-empty subsets** $(X, Y)$ of the 4 attributes. Assign each attribute to $X$, $Y$ or neither ($3^4$ ways) and remove the cases with $X$ or $Y$ empty by inclusion–exclusion.

steps.title: Model an FD as a 3-way labelling
steps.body:
Since $X\cap Y=\emptyset$, every attribute is in exactly one of: $X$, $Y$, or neither. Each such labelling gives exactly one pair $(X,Y)$:
$$3^4=81\ \text{labellings}.$$

steps.title: Remove empty X or empty Y
steps.body:
$X=\emptyset$: each attribute is in $Y$ or neither → $2^4=16$. Likewise $Y=\emptyset$: $16$. Both empty: $1$ (counted in both).
$$81-16-16+1=50.$$

steps.title: Cross-check by the size of X
steps.body:
Choose $X$ with $\lvert X\rvert=k$, then $Y$ is any non-empty subset of the other $4-k$ attributes: $\binom4k(2^{4-k}-1)$.
$$\binom41\cdot7+\binom42\cdot3+\binom43\cdot1+\binom44\cdot0=28+18+4+0=50.$$

pitfalls: Counting all pairs of non-empty subsets $(2^4-1)^2=225$ — ignores the disjointness condition.
Forgetting to add back the case where both are empty (gives 49).
Treating $X \to Y$ and $Y \to X$ as the same FD — they are different dependencies, so the pair is ordered.
cse-2024-2-cs-46.verification: Both the inclusion–exclusion count and the case split by $\lvert X\rvert$ give 50. Small check with $n=2$ attributes $\{A,B\}$: formula $9-8+1=2$ ($A\to B$, $B\to A$) — correct.

animation.title: Useful FDs by size of X

cse-2024-2-cs-47.approach: Size every field from its count ($\lceil\log_2\rceil$ bits), subtract from 32 to get the opcode width, then opcodes $=2^{\text{width}}$. The addressing-mode field is separate, so every opcode works with every mode.

steps.title: Register and addressing-mode fields
steps.body:
16 registers → $\log_2 16=4$ bits per register field; two fields → $2\times4=8$ bits.
8 addressing modes → $\log_2 8=3$ bits.

steps.title: Opcode width
steps.body: $$32-16-8-3=5\ \text{bits for the opcode}.$$

steps.title: Number of opcodes
steps.body: A 5-bit opcode encodes $2^5=32$ distinct opcodes. The 3-bit mode field is independent of the opcode, so each of the 32 opcodes is available with every one of the 8 addressing modes: **32**.

pitfalls: Multiplying by the modes ($32\times8=256$): that counts opcode–mode combinations, not opcodes per mode.
Using 16 registers as 16 bits, or forgetting one of the two register fields.
cse-2024-2-cs-47.verification: Field sum: $5+3+4+4+16=32$ bits — the format is fully used, so 5 is the maximum opcode width.

cse-2024-2-cs-48.approach: Both designs run at the same 2 GHz clock, so speedup is simply the ratio of CPIs: 6 for the non-pipelined unit versus $1+$ (average stall cycles per instruction) for the pipeline.

steps.title: Average stall cycles per instruction
steps.body: $$0.2\times2+0.2\times3=0.4+0.6=1.0\ \text{cycle per instruction}.$$

steps.title: Pipelined CPI
steps.body:
Ideal CPI is 1, so
$$\text{CPI}_{\text{pipe}}=1+1.0=2.$$

steps.title: Speedup
steps.body:
Clock period is identical ($0.5$ ns), so
$$\text{Speedup}=\frac{6\times0.5\ \text{ns}}{2\times0.5\ \text{ns}}=\frac{6}{2}=3.0.$$

pitfalls: Using the number of stages (5) as the non-pipelined CPI gives 2.5 — the question says the unit takes 6 cycles per instruction.
Applying each stall to all instructions ($1+2+3=6$) gives speedup 1 — only 20% of instructions incur each stall.
Ignoring stalls gives the ideal speedup 6.
cse-2024-2-cs-48.verification: Per 100 instructions: non-pipelined $600$ cycles; pipelined $100+20\times2+20\times3=200$ cycles; $600/200=3.0$.

cse-2024-2-cs-49.approach: Kruskal view: all MSTs take the same number of edges of each weight, and the choices inside one weight class are independent. Take every weight-1 edge, then count how many ways the weight-2 edges can join the remaining components without a cycle.
cse-2024-2-cs-49.given:
| weight | edges |
|---|---|
| 1 | a–b, a–f, c–d, d–e |
| 2 | a–g, b–g, f–g, g–c, g–d, g–e |
| 3 | b–c, f–e |

steps.title: Weight 1: all four edges are forced
steps.body:
$a\text{–}b$, $a\text{–}f$, $c\text{–}d$, $d\text{–}e$ form no cycle, so every MST contains all four (Kruskal adds them in any order). Components now:
$$\{a,b,f\},\quad\{c,d,e\},\quad\{g\}.$$

steps.title: Weight 2, left side: 3 equivalent choices
steps.body: $a\text{–}g$, $b\text{–}g$, $f\text{–}g$ all join $\{g\}$ to $\{a,b,f\}$. Exactly **one** of them can be taken: a second one would close a cycle through $\{a,b,f\}$. → **3 choices**.

steps.title: Weight 2, right side: 3 equivalent choices
steps.body: $g\text{–}c$, $g\text{–}d$, $g\text{–}e$ all join $\{g\}$ to $\{c,d,e\}$; exactly one can be taken. → **3 choices**. The left and right choices are independent.

steps.title: Weight 3 edges are never needed
steps.body:
After one left and one right weight-2 edge, all 7 vertices are connected with $4+2=6=7-1$ edges. Edges $b\text{–}c$ and $f\text{–}e$ (weight 3) would close cycles, so no MST uses them.
MST weight $=4\times1+2\times2=8$; one example: $\{ab, af, cd, de, ag, gd\}$.

steps.title: Count
steps.body: $$\#\text{MST}=3\times3=9.$$

cse-2024-2-cs-49.shortcut: Contract the weight-1 edges: you get a star with centre $g$ and two super-nodes, each joined to $g$ by 3 parallel weight-2 edges → $3	imes3=9$.
pitfalls: Counting all $\binom{6}{2}=15$ pairs of weight-2 edges — two edges on the same side (e.g. $a\text{–}g$ and $b\text{–}g$) form a cycle with $a\text{–}b$.
Thinking a weight-3 edge can replace a weight-2 edge: it would increase the total weight above 8.
Adding the two sides ($3+3=6$) instead of multiplying: the choices are independent.
cse-2024-2-cs-49.verification: Check the minimum weight: 7 vertices need 6 edges; only 4 edges have weight 1, so at least $4\times1+2\times2=8$; each of the 9 trees reaches 8, and any tree using a weight-3 edge or fewer weight-1 edges weighs more.

cse-2024-2-cs-50.approach: Number the 8 vertices around the octagon. Every edge joins two vertices whose positions differ by an odd amount (1 or 3 steps), so "even positions" vs "odd positions" is a proper 2-colouring — the graph is bipartite (in fact $K_{4,4}$).

steps.title: Label the vertices around the octagon
steps.body: Go clockwise from the top-left vertex: $v_0$ (top-left), $v_1$ (top-right), $v_2$, $v_3$ (right side), $v_4$, $v_5$ (bottom), $v_6$, $v_7$ (left side). There are 16 edges and every vertex has degree 4.

steps.title: Every edge joins positions an odd distance apart
steps.body:
| edges | step distance |
|---|---|
| 8 octagon sides $v_iv_{i+1}$ | 1 |
| horizontals $v_7v_2$, $v_6v_3$ | 3 |
| verticals $v_0v_5$, $v_1v_4$ | 3 |
| diagonals $v_0v_3$, $v_1v_6$, $v_7v_4$, $v_2v_5$ | 3 |

So each edge joins an **even**-indexed vertex to an **odd**-indexed one. Each even vertex is adjacent to all 4 odd vertices (e.g. $v_0$: $v_1, v_7, v_5, v_3$): the graph is $K_{4,4}$.

steps.title: Two colours suffice and are necessary
steps.body:
Colour $\{v_0,v_2,v_4,v_6\}$ blue and $\{v_1,v_3,v_5,v_7\}$ orange: no edge has both ends the same colour. One colour is impossible because the graph has edges. Hence
$$\chi(G)=2.$$

cse-2024-2-cs-50.shortcut: A graph is 2-colourable iff it has no odd cycle. Here all edges connect alternate classes around the octagon, so no odd cycle exists.
pitfalls: Being misled by the many crossings and the "star" look into answering 3 or 4 — crossings are irrelevant to colouring.
Assuming the crossing diagonals create triangles: e.g. $v_0, v_1, v_3$ is not a triangle because $v_1v_3$ is not an edge.
cse-2024-2-cs-50.verification: Edge count check: $K_{4,4}$ has $4\times4=16$ edges and is 4-regular — exactly what the figure shows (16 edges, each vertex of degree 4).

cse-2024-2-cs-51.approach: Find the opcode width from 75 operations per type plus the type bit, the register width from 50 registers, then fill the rest of the 32 bits in each format.

steps.title: OPCODE width Y
steps.body:
150 instructions split equally → 75 R-type and 75 I-type. One OPCODE bit tells the type; the rest must distinguish 75 operations:
$$\lceil\log_2 75\rceil=7\quad(2^6=64<75\le128=2^7)\ \Rightarrow\ Y=1+7=8.$$

steps.title: Register field width
steps.body: 50 registers need $\lceil\log_2 50\rceil=6$ bits ($2^5=32<50\le64$). All register fields are 6 bits.

cse-2024-2-cs-51.shortcut: From the two formats, $X=32-Y-18$ and $Z=32-Y-12$, so $X+2Y+Z=64-30=34$ — independent of $Y$.
pitfalls: Using $\lceil\log_2150\rceil=8$ bits for the operation part plus the type bit ($Y=9$): $Y$ changes, but $X$ and $Z$ shrink with it, and the sum is still 34 (the expression is designed to be robust).
Taking register width as $\log_2 50\approx5.6\to5$ bits: 5 bits address only 32 registers.
Forgetting that the R-type has three register fields but the I-type only two.
cse-2024-2-cs-51.verification: R-type: $8+6+6+6+6=32$; I-type: $8+6+6+12=32$. Both formats fill exactly 32 bits.

cse-2024-2-cs-52.approach: Recognise $L_1$: $b^*ab^*$ contributes one $a$, each $(ab^*ab^*)$ adds two more, and $b$'s may appear anywhere — so $L_1$ is exactly the strings with an **odd number of $a$'s**. Then count such strings of each length $\le4$.

steps.title: L1 = strings with an odd number of a
steps.body: Every word of $b^*ab^*(ab^*ab^*)^*$ has $1+2m$ $a$'s (odd). Conversely, a string with $2m+1$ $a$'s splits as $b^{i_0}ab^{i_1}\ \cdot\ (ab^{i_2}ab^{i_3})\cdots$: the first $a$ with its surrounding $b$'s matches $b^*ab^*$ and the remaining $a$'s pair up into $ab^*ab^*$ blocks. So $L_1$ is recognised by the 2-state parity DFA.

steps.title: Count by length
steps.body:
Strings of length $n$ with an odd number of $a$'s: $\sum_{k\ \text{odd}}\binom nk=2^{n-1}$ for $n\ge1$, and $0$ for $n=0$ ($\varepsilon$ has zero $a$'s).

$n=1$: $1$ ($a$); $n=2$: $\binom21=2$; $n=3$: $\binom31+\binom33=4$; $n=4$: $\binom41+\binom43=8$.

steps.title: Total
steps.body:
$L_2$ contains every string of length $0$ to $4$, so $L_1\cap L_2$ is the set of odd-$a$ strings of length at most 4:
$$\underbrace{0}_{n=0}+\underbrace{1}_{n=1}+\underbrace{2}_{n=2}+\underbrace{4}_{n=3}+\underbrace{8}_{n=4}=15.$$

cse-2024-2-cs-52.shortcut: Exactly half of the $2^n$ strings of each length $n\ge1$ have odd parity of $a$: $\frac{2+4+8+16}{2}=15$.
pitfalls: Reading $L_1$ as "odd length" or "exactly one $a$": strings with 3 $a$'s such as $aaab$ are in $L_1$ too.
Counting $\varepsilon$ — it has zero (even) $a$'s, so it is not in $L_1$.
cse-2024-2-cs-52.verification: Complement check: strings of length $\le4$ total $1+2+4+8+16=31$; even-$a$ strings are $1+1+2+4+8=16$; $31-16=15$.

cse-2024-2-cs-53.approach: In a direct product the inverse is taken componentwise, so $(x,y,z)$ is its own inverse iff $2x\equiv0\ (2)$, $2y\equiv0\ (3)$ and $2z\equiv0\ (4)$. Count the solutions in each factor and multiply.

steps.title: Condition componentwise
steps.body: $(x,y,z)^{-1}=(-x,-y,-z)$, so $(x,y,z)$ is self-inverse iff $x+x\equiv0\pmod2$, $y+y\equiv0\pmod3$, $z+z\equiv0\pmod4$.

steps.title: Solve in each factor
steps.body:
- $Z_2$: $2x\equiv0\pmod 2$ for every $x$ → $\{0,1\}$: **2**.
- $Z_3$: $2y\equiv0\pmod 3$ only for $y=0$ ($2\cdot1=2$, $2\cdot2=4\equiv1$) → **1**.
- $Z_4$: $2z\equiv0\pmod4$ for $z=0$ and $z=2$ ($2\cdot1=2$, $2\cdot3=6\equiv2$) → **2**.

cse-2024-2-cs-53.shortcut: Self-inverse elements = identity + elements of order 2. $Z_2\times Z_3\times Z_4\cong Z_3\times(Z_2\times Z_4)$; the 2-part $Z_2\times Z_4$ has $2\cdot2=4$ solutions of $2g=0$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the identity $(0,0,0)$ — it is its own inverse (answer 3 is wrong).
Counting $1$ in $Z_4$ as self-inverse: $1+1=2\ne0$ in $Z_4$; its inverse is 3.
cse-2024-2-cs-53.verification: List check: the four elements each satisfy $g+g=0$: e.g. $(1,0,2)+(1,0,2)=(2,0,4)\equiv(0,0,0)$. Any element with $y\ne0$ fails since $2y\not\equiv0\pmod3$.

animation.title: Solutions of g + g = 0 in each factor

cse-2024-2-cs-54.approach: Split the 20-bit page number into 10 + 10 bits: one inner page-table page maps 1024 consecutive pages (4 MB). The outer directory is always 1 page; inner pages are minimum when the 2000 pages are packed, maximum when they are spread one-per-region (capped by the 1024 directory entries).
cse-2024-2-cs-54.given:
| Item | Value |
|---|---|
| virtual address | 32 bits |
| page | 4 KB = $2^{12}$ B |
| PTE | 4 B |
| pages touched | 2000 |

steps.title: Address split
steps.body: Offset $=12$ bits, so the page number has $32-12=20$ bits. One page holds $\frac{4096}{4}=1024=2^{10}$ PTEs, so the 20 bits split as 10 (directory index) $+$ 10 (inner index). The directory has $2^{10}$ entries $\times4$ B $=4$ KB $=$ **1 page**.

steps.title: Minimum X: pack the pages
steps.body:
One inner page covers 1024 consecutive virtual pages. 2000 pages need at least
$$\left\lceil\frac{2000}{1024}\right\rceil=2\ \text{inner pages}\ \Rightarrow\ X=1+2=3.$$

steps.title: Maximum Y: spread the pages
steps.body:
Each touched page could lie in a different 4 MB region, but there are only $2^{10}=1024$ regions (directory entries). So at most $\min(2000,1024)=1024$ inner pages:
$$Y=1+1024=1025.$$

pitfalls: Taking $Y=1+2000$: there are only 1024 possible inner page tables in a 32-bit space with this split.
Forgetting the outer page directory page in X or Y (gives 1026).
Using $\lfloor2000/1024\rfloor=1$ for the minimum — 1024 PTEs cannot map 2000 pages.
cse-2024-2-cs-54.verification: Coverage check: 2 inner pages map $2048\ge2000$ pages, 1 maps only 1024; 1024 inner pages cover the full $2^{20}$-page space, the absolute maximum.

animation.title: Pages used by the 2-level page table

cse-2024-2-cs-55.approach: Write $I_0$, move the dot over $S$ in every item that has $\bullet S$ (the kernel), then take the closure of that kernel. Count the items.

steps.title: Items of I0 with the dot before S
steps.body: $I_0=\text{CLOSURE}(\{S'\to\bullet S\})$ contains $S'\to\bullet S$, all five $S\to\bullet\ldots$ items, $A\to\bullet d\#$ and $B\to\bullet @$ (8 items). Only two have the dot before $S$: $S'\to\bullet S$ and $S\to\bullet SS$.

steps.title: Kernel of GOTO(I0, S)
steps.body:
Advance the dot over $S$:
$$S'\to S\bullet,\qquad S\to S\bullet S.$$

steps.title: Closure: dot before S
steps.body: $S\to S\bullet S$ has the dot before the non-terminal $S$, so add all $S$-productions with the dot at the start: $S\to\bullet SS$, $S\to\bullet Aa$, $S\to\bullet bAc$, $S\to\bullet Bc$, $S\to\bullet bBa$ (5 items; $S\to\bullet SS$ adds nothing new).

steps.title: Closure: dot before A and B
steps.body:
$S\to\bullet Aa$ adds $A\to\bullet d\#$; $S\to\bullet Bc$ adds $B\to\bullet @$. In $S\to\bullet bAc$ and $S\to\bullet bBa$ the dot is before the terminal $b$, so they add nothing.
$$2+5+2=9\ \text{items}.$$

cse-2024-2-cs-55.shortcut: $\text{GOTO}(I_0,S)$ $=$ the two kernel items $+$ everything in $I_0$ except $S'\to\bullet S$ (because the new kernel $S\to S\bullet S$ regenerates the closure of $S$): $2+(8-1)=9$.
pitfalls: Forgetting the nested closure items $A\to\bullet d\#$ and $B\to\bullet @$ (gives 7).
Stopping at the kernel (2 items) — the dot before $S$ in $S\to S\bullet S$ forces a closure.
Adding $A\to\bullet d\#$ again because of $S\to\bullet bAc$: there the dot is before $b$, not $A$; and duplicates are counted once anyway.
cse-2024-2-cs-55.verification: Cross-check with the shortcut: $I_0$ has 8 items; GOTO keeps the 7 non-start closure items and adds 2 kernel items: $7+2=9$.

cols: why it is in the set
